questions.stem: Which of the following is an internal economy of scale?
options: Bulk buying reducing the cost per unit of raw materials
A pool of skilled labour developing in the local area
Better transport links built because the industry grew
Specialist suppliers setting up nearby
questions.why: Internal economies come from the individual business growing. Purchasing, technical, managerial, financial and marketing economies are the standard five.
whyNot: That is external: the industry grew, not this firm.
External.
External.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of external economies of scale?
options: Cost advantages arising from the growth of the whole industry in an area
Cost advantages arising from the growth of the individual business
The rise in average cost when a business grows too large
Savings from buying inputs in bulk
questions.why: The individual business benefits without having grown itself: trained local labour, nearby specialist suppliers, better infrastructure.
whyNot: Those are internal economies.
Those are diseconomies of scale.
That is a purchasing economy, which is internal.

questions.stem: Which term describes lower cost per unit from using large specialised equipment more fully?
options: Technical economies
Purchasing economies
Managerial economies
Financial economies
questions.why: Large specialised machinery is only worth buying at high volume, and larger plant is often proportionately cheaper to run.
whyNot: Purchasing economies come from bulk buying inputs.
Managerial economies come from employing specialists whose cost is spread over more output.
Financial economies come from borrowing more cheaply.

questions.stem: How does growth reduce supplier power?
options: A larger buyer can demand lower prices, longer credit and priority supply
Suppliers are forced to merge
The business no longer needs any suppliers
Suppliers become legally obliged to cut prices
questions.why: Size gives negotiating leverage, which is often the real motive behind growth. It links directly to Porter's five forces.
whyNot: Growth does not force supplier consolidation.
Inputs are still needed.
No legal obligation exists.

questions.stem: Why is higher revenue from growth not the same as higher profit?
options: Costs may rise faster than revenue, for example through diseconomies of scale
Revenue and profit are always equal
Growth never affects revenue
Profit is calculated before costs
questions.why: Growth can raise revenue while raising costs faster, or raise total profit while reducing profit per unit. Saying so is a reliable evaluation point on any growth question.
whyNot: Profit is revenue minus costs.
Growth normally raises revenue; the issue is what happens to costs.
Profit is revenue after costs.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures why growth should not be pursued for its own sake?
options: Growth is a means to lower costs, market power and profit, and it delivers none of those automatically
Growth is always harmful to a business
Growth is only possible for large businesses
Growth always requires a takeover
questions.why: If growth does not reduce unit costs, or outruns the cash, or passes the optimum size, it destroys value. Asking what the growth is FOR is the mark of a strong answer.
whyNot: Growth is often beneficial; the point is that it is not automatic.
Small businesses grow constantly.
Organic growth requires no acquisition.

questions.stem: Why are economies of scale genuine but limited for a small guesthouse group?
options: Purchasing and managerial savings are real, but the property itself does not get cheaper per room with scale
There are no economies of scale in services
Small businesses cannot buy in bulk
Economies of scale only apply to manufacturing
questions.why: One booking system, one marketing effort and bulk food purchasing all save money. The largest cost, the buildings, scales roughly in proportion, so the total saving is smaller than in manufacturing.
whyNot: Service businesses do achieve economies, particularly in marketing and administration.
They can, and the saving is capped by the size of the local market.
They apply across all sectors, in differing degrees.

questions.stem: Which is the key financial question when assessing a growth plan?
options: Whether the business can finance the growth without running out of cash
Whether the owner wants to grow
Whether competitors are growing
Whether the market is large
questions.why: Growth consumes cash before it generates it, which is where most growth plans fail. Checking the cash is the first practical test of any growth proposal.
whyNot: Relevant, and it is a question about objectives rather than finance.
Relevant context, not the financial test.
Relevant to the opportunity, not to affordability.
